name: Continental
how: Hold the racket as if shaking hands with it on its edge, or as you would hold a hammer. Index knuckle and heel pad both sit on bevel 2 (right-handers).
contact: Low to waist height; racket face naturally open
pros: One grip for the whole net game and the serve: no grip changes under pressure
Allows pronation on the serve for spin and power
cons: Hard to generate topspin on groundstrokes
Forehand face opens on high balls
Modern players rarely use it for forehands
users: Every pro on serve and volley
Roger Federer and Ashleigh Barty on the slice
tip: If your serve has no spin, this grip is usually the missing piece.

name: Eastern forehand
how: Shake hands with the racket face: index knuckle and heel pad on bevel 3.
contact: Waist height; the most comfortable grip for low and medium balls
pros: Easiest grip to learn: the hand is flat behind the handle
Lets you hit flat and take the ball early
Quick change to Continental for volleys
tip: The grip for players who want to attack and move forward.

name: Semi-Western forehand
how: Rotate the hand one bevel further under the handle: index knuckle and heel pad on bevel 4.
shots: Top hand of a two-handed backhand (many players)
contact: Waist to shoulder height, in front of the body
pros: The best balance of topspin and power
Used by most of the top 100
cons: Low balls and slice need extra knee bend
Needs a bigger grip change to volley
tip: If you only learn one forehand grip, learn this one.

name: Western forehand
how: Hand fully under the handle: index knuckle and heel pad on bevel 5. Lay the racket flat on the ground and pick it up.
pros: Maximum topspin: huge net clearance and safety
cons: Very difficult on low balls and fast courts
Wrist strain if the technique is poor
tip: Great on clay and for juniors who hit heavy; a handicap on grass or indoors.

name: Eastern backhand
how: Index knuckle and heel pad on bevel 1, the top of the handle. The knuckles face the net at contact.
contact: Waist height, far in front with a straight arm
pros: Beautiful, long lever: easy power and reach
Flows into the slice with a small change
cons: Needs an early preparation and a strong shoulder turn
Return of big serves is tougher
tip: Strong Eastern (between bevels 1 and 8) gives more topspin: Wawrinka and Thiem use it.

name: Two-handed backhand
how: Bottom (dominant) hand holds Continental on bevel 2. Top (non-dominant) hand holds an Eastern or Semi-Western forehand grip (bevel 3 or 4) above it, hands touching.
contact: Waist to chest height, in front; the top hand hits a left-handed forehand
pros: Stability and power from both arms
Best grip for returning big serves and high balls
cons: Needs more footwork to get to wide balls
Slice still needs a one-handed Continental
tip: Think of it as a left-handed forehand with the right hand along for the ride.
